newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian media pay fulsome tribute to Deng. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Asian media pay fulsome tribute to Deng. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]

text.p: Asian media on Friday sounded more glowing tributes to Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping, focusing their praise on his economic achievements and playing down his role in crushing political dissent.
Hong Kong newspapers were effusive, with many eulogising his reformist policies that made China rich and strong.

"Nobody in the course of this century raised the material standards of living of more people than Deng Xiaoping," the widely circulated South China Morning Post said of Deng, 92, who died on Wednesday.
The territory's normally trim Beijing-backed newspapers, Wen Wei Pao and Ta Kung Pao, boasted separate takeouts filled with condolence advertisements from companies and individuals.
China's propaganda machine went into overdrive, hailing the diminutive Deng as a giant whose stature could never be matched and pledging the army's loyalty to his political heirs.
"Comrade Deng Xiaoping ... became a great son of the people, a giant who will never be matched," the People's Daily said in a commentary. "The people of the motherland love and esteem him."
In Japan, Tokyo's Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper described Deng as "a realist who made use of the monolithic rule of the Communist Party and put priority on stability".
The Japan Times said Deng would be remembered as a "master tactician whose humility and mild demeanor belied the power and authority he exercised".

But it added: "He was also the unrepentant Communist Party chief who set the People's Liberation Army against the students and demonstrators who occupied Tiananmen Square ... Deng's willingness to reform the Maoist system only went so far."

In Taiwan, some 55 percent of 888 people interviewed by Taipei's United Daily News said they were positive about Deng's contribution to Chinese history, compared with a scant nine percent who said Deng did not make any contribution at all.
Another newspaper poll conducted by the China Times showed that 42 percent of 972 respondents said Deng's contribution was greater than that of Mao Zedong.

Singapore's Straits Times said Deng was "one of the great men of the 20th century" and could one day be judged "China's most inspired leader" despite his 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy activists in Tiananmen Square.
Singapore's Business Times sounded a note of caution, however, saying Deng's death could slow down China's economy as President Jiang Zemin compromises on key issues to keep his job.

"The situation is near critical on many fronts -- loss-making state enterprises, under-investment in the agricultural sector, overbuilding in the cities, lack of a uniform body of business legislation, corruption, to name but a few," wrote columnist Lee Han Shih
"If the economy is to continue to grow, Mr Jiang and his team need to tackle these problems immediately," he said.

This view was shared by India's The Hindu newspaper. In his column Sujit Dutta, senior fellow at the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses, said: "Politically and economically China is stable and Deng's delayed death has stabilised Jiang Zemin and his reformist group.
"But hereafter the leadership will have to cope with the huge theoretical and structural problems of the reforms in this vast country on its own."
The Financial Express described Deng's economic reforms as irreversible, a view shared by Pakistan's Dawn.
In Sydney, the Australian Fiancial Review also chose to focus on Deng's economic achievements.

"Perhaps no other individual in human history delivered a larger and more widespread increase in material wealth than the paramount ruler of China, who died yesterday," the daily said in its editorial.
Thailand's English-language Bangkok Post said Deng would be remembered as the architect who liberalised China's economy and enabled it to become a member of the international community.
Sri Lankan media described Deng as a visionary and pragmatic leader whose economic reforms propelled his country along a path of rapid development.
Colombo's independent Island newspaper (corrects name) said in an editorial that the most outstanding feature of this "unrepentant communist" was his pragmatism.
